paragraphs.text: הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָזָ֔ה יְשַֽׁעְיָ֖הוּ בֶּן־אָמ֑וֹץ עַל־יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

i18n.en: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.
i18n.he: הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָזָ֔ה יְשַֽׁעְיָ֖הוּ בֶּן־אָמ֑וֹץ עַל־יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

notes.official: *haddāḇār ʾăšer ḥāzāh yᵉšaʿyāhû ben-ʾāmôṣ* “The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw” is a second superscription after 1:1. It introduces the collection that runs to 4:6 (Wildberger, *Isaiah 1–12*, Continental, 1991; Williamson, *Isaiah 1–5*, ICC, 2006). *ḥāzāh* is the verb of prophetic vision, and a “word” that is “seen” is the book’s idiom for received revelation (compare *ḥăzôn* at 1:1). The line keeps the collocation literally.

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בְּאַחֲרִ֣ית הַיָּמִ֗ים נָכ֨וֹן יִֽהְיֶ֜ה הַ֤ר בֵּית־יְהוָה֙ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ הֶהָרִ֔ים וְנִשָּׂ֖א מִגְּבָע֑וֹת וְנָהֲר֥וּ אֵלָ֖יו כָּל־הַגּוֹיִֽם׃

i18n.en: And it shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of YHWH shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it.
i18n.he: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בְּאַחֲרִ֣ית הַיָּמִ֗ים נָכ֨וֹן יִֽהְיֶ֜ה הַ֤ר בֵּית־יְהוָה֙ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ הֶהָרִ֔ים וְנִשָּׂ֖א מִגְּבָע֑וֹת וְנָהֲר֥וּ אֵלָ֖יו כָּל־הַגּוֹיִֽם׃

notes.official:
Isa 2:2–4 is also carried by Micah (Mic 4:1–3), with small differences of wording. micah-woh has no chapter 4 yet, so the wording fixed here is the shared rendering for both books (central `isa-2-2-4-mic-4-1-3-zion-pilgrimage-parallel-cross-corpus`, new). Mic 4:1 has the same clauses in a slightly different order and reads “peoples” (*ʿammîm*) where Isaiah has “all the nations.”

*bᵉrōʾš hehārîm* is “on the top of the mountains” (ASV). The preposition can also express rank: “as the highest of the mountains” (NRSV), “above the mountains” (NJPS). The line keeps the spatial sense, the plain meaning of *bᵉ-* with *rōʾš*; the rank reading stays audible in “lifted up above the hills.” *wᵉnāhărû* “shall flow” is the verb derived from *nāhār* “river” (BDB; HALOT *nhr* I), so the nations stream uphill to the mountain, an image most commentators take as deliberate (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp, *Isaiah 1–39*, AB 19, 2000). NJPS “shall gaze on it with joy” takes *nhr* II “be radiant” (Jer 31:12; Ps 34:6); the line follows ASV and NRSV (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

*bᵉʾaḥărîṯ hayyāmîm* “in the latter days” is rendered under the central `be-acharit-ha-yamim-latter-days-temporal-eschatological-horizon-cross-corpus` entry. That entry records the historical-future and the eschatological readings without choosing between them.

paragraphs.text: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֗ים וְאָמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹרֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיּוֹן֙ תֵּצֵ֣א תוֹרָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

i18n.en: And many peoples shall go and say: “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of YHWH, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us of his ways, and that we may walk in his paths.” For out of Zion shall go forth teaching, and the word of YHWH from Jerusalem.
i18n.he: וְֽהָלְכ֞וּ עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֗ים וְאָמְרוּ֙ לְכ֣וּ ׀ וְנַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְיֹרֵ֙נוּ֙ מִדְּרָכָ֔יו וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּאֹרְחֹתָ֑יו כִּ֤י מִצִּיּוֹן֙ תֵּצֵ֣א תוֹרָ֔ה וּדְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

notes.official:
The peoples’ speech is closed after “his paths” (NRSV, NJPS; ASV prints no quotation marks). The *kî*-clause “For out of Zion shall go forth teaching” is then the prophet’s statement of why they come. It can also be read as the last words of the peoples; the Hebrew has no marker either way, and the punctuation follows the modern versions.

*wᵉyōrēnû* “that he may teach us” and *tôrāh* “teaching” come from the same root, *yrh* “direct, instruct,” and the line gives both a teaching-word so the link stays visible. ASV has “law.” The rendering follows overlay `torah-teaching-isaiah`, whose rationale already cites this verse; 2:3 is added to its appliesTo. *middᵉrāḵāyw* “of his ways” keeps the partitive *min* (ASV). *ʾĕlōhê yaʿăqōḇ* “the God of Jacob” follows the construct-epithet rule of overlay `elohei-yisrael-god-of-israel-isaiah-24`. This wording is the shared rendering for Mic 4:2 (central `isa-2-2-4-mic-4-1-3-zion-pilgrimage-parallel-cross-corpus`).

paragraphs.text: וְשָׁפַט֙ בֵּ֣ין הַגּוֹיִ֔ם וְהוֹכִ֖יחַ לְעַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבוֹתָ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֽוֹתֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵר֔וֹת לֹא־יִשָּׂ֨א ג֤וֹי אֶל־גּוֹי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּ ע֖וֹד מִלְחָמָֽה׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And he shall judge between the nations, and shall decide for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any more.
i18n.he: וְשָׁפַט֙ בֵּ֣ין הַגּוֹיִ֔ם וְהוֹכִ֖יחַ לְעַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים וְכִתְּת֨וּ חַרְבוֹתָ֜ם לְאִתִּ֗ים וַחֲנִיתֽוֹתֵיהֶם֙ לְמַזְמֵר֔וֹת לֹא־יִשָּׂ֨א ג֤וֹי אֶל־גּוֹי֙ חֶ֔רֶב וְלֹא־יִלְמְד֥וּ ע֖וֹד מִלְחָמָֽה׃ (פ)

notes.official:
*wᵉhôḵîaḥ lᵉʿammîm rabbîm* “and shall decide for many peoples”: the Hiphil of *ykḥ* with *lᵉ-* is to settle a dispute for the parties, to arbitrate (BDB; HALOT; NRSV and NJPS “arbitrate for”). The line keeps “decide for,” close to ASV “decide concerning.” *ʾittîm* is “plowshares” (ASV, NRSV, NJPS). The exact implement is uncertain (ploughshare, mattock or hoe have all been proposed); the point is that weapons become farm tools. *mazmērôṯ* are “pruning hooks.” Joel 4:10 (Eng. 3:10) reverses the image: “Beat your plowshares into swords.”

Mic 4:3 has the pair the other way round (“between many peoples … for strong nations afar off”) and continues with a verse Isaiah lacks (Mic 4:4, each under his vine and fig tree). The wording here is the shared rendering for the clauses the two books have in common (central `isa-2-2-4-mic-4-1-3-zion-pilgrimage-parallel-cross-corpus`; overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

paragraphs.text: בֵּ֖ית יַעֲקֹ֑ב לְכ֥וּ וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּא֥וֹר יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: O house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of YHWH.
i18n.he: בֵּ֖ית יַעֲקֹ֑ב לְכ֥וּ וְנֵלְכָ֖ה בְּא֥וֹר יְהוָֽה׃

notes.official: The call to “the house of Jacob” turns the vision of vv. 2–4 into an appeal to Judah and opens the unit of vv. 5–22. Micah’s parallel goes another way here (Mic 4:5, “For all the peoples walk each in the name of its god”), so the shared rendering covers vv. 2–4 only (central `isa-2-2-4-mic-4-1-3-zion-pilgrimage-parallel-cross-corpus` does not extend to this verse).

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י נָטַ֗שְׁתָּה עַמְּךָ֙ בֵּ֣ית יַעֲקֹ֔ב כִּ֤י מָלְאוּ֙ מִקֶּ֔דֶם וְעֹֽנְנִ֖ים כַּפְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וּבְיַלְדֵ֥י נָכְרִ֖ים יַשְׂפִּֽיקוּ׃

i18n.en: For you have forsaken your people, the house of Jacob, because they are full from the east, and are soothsayers like the Philistines, and they strike hands with the children of foreigners.
i18n.he: כִּ֣י נָטַ֗שְׁתָּה עַמְּךָ֙ בֵּ֣ית יַעֲקֹ֔ב כִּ֤י מָלְאוּ֙ מִקֶּ֔דֶם וְעֹֽנְנִ֖ים כַּפְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וּבְיַלְדֵ֥י נָכְרִ֖ים יַשְׂפִּֽיקוּ׃

notes.official:
Three cruxes. (1) *kî mālᵉʾû miqqedem* “because they are full from the east” is elliptical: something is missing after “full.” ASV supplies “[with customs]” and NJPS “[of practices],” and many commentators emend to *qōsᵉmîm* “diviners” (Wildberger; BHS apparatus). The line keeps the bare MT and supplies nothing.

(2) *wᵉʿōnᵉnîm kappᵉlištîm* “and are soothsayers like the Philistines.” The Poel of *ʿnn* names a forbidden practice of divination (Lev 19:26; Deut 18:10, 14; 2 Kgs 21:6), rendered “soothsayers” as at micah-woh 5:11 (central `onen-soothsayer-cross-corpus`, new). Its derivation is disputed. Proposals include *ʿānān* “cloud” (“reading the clouds”), a sound-word for humming or crooning, and *ʿayin* “eye” (BDB; HALOT; Jeffers, *Magic and Divination in Ancient Palestine and Syria*, 1996). None is established, so the line keeps the general term.

(3) *ûḇᵉyaldê noḵrîm yaśpîqû* “and they strike hands with the children of foreigners” takes *spq* I “clap, strike [hands]” (ASV; compare Job 27:23), the gesture that seals a bargain. NJPS takes *spq* II “abound” (“they abound in customs of the aliens”). The line follows ASV without its supplement. *nāṭaštāh ʿammᵉḵā* “you have forsaken your people” addresses YHWH directly; the LXX has the third person (“he has abandoned his people”). The line keeps MT (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

**Lens-salient site (apparatus note, not a translation claim).** If *ʿōnᵉnîm* came from *ʿānān*, the practice would be the reading of signs in the sky. That is one of three proposed derivations, and the line does not use it. The canon does not cite this verse.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּמָּלֵ֤א אַרְצוֹ֙ כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֔ב וְאֵ֥ין קֵ֖צֶה לְאֹצְרֹתָ֑יו וַתִּמָּלֵ֤א אַרְצוֹ֙ סוּסִ֔ים וְאֵ֥ין קֵ֖צֶה לְמַרְכְּבֹתָֽיו׃

i18n.en: Their land is full of silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is full of horses, and there is no end to their chariots.
i18n.he: וַתִּמָּלֵ֤א אַרְצוֹ֙ כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֔ב וְאֵ֥ין קֵ֖צֶה לְאֹצְרֹתָ֑יו וַתִּמָּלֵ֤א אַרְצוֹ֙ סוּסִ֔ים וְאֵ֥ין קֵ֖צֶה לְמַרְכְּבֹתָֽיו׃

notes.official: *ʾarṣô* “their land” (a singular suffix referring to the house of Jacob) is a territory, rendered under the central `eretz` entry. The goods listed, silver and gold, horses and chariots, are those the law of the king restricts (Deut 17:16–17; Wildberger).

paragraphs.text: וַתִּמָּלֵ֥א אַרְצ֖וֹ אֱלִילִ֑ים לְמַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדָיו֙ יִֽשְׁתַּחֲו֔וּ לַאֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשׂ֖וּ אֶצְבְּעֹתָֽיו׃

i18n.en: Their land is full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their fingers have made.
i18n.he: וַתִּמָּלֵ֥א אַרְצ֖וֹ אֱלִילִ֑ים לְמַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדָיו֙ יִֽשְׁתַּחֲו֔וּ לַאֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשׂ֖וּ אֶצְבְּעֹתָֽיו׃

notes.official: *ʾĕlîlîm* “idols” is Isaiah’s characteristic word for the images of other gods (2:8, 18, 20; 10:10–11; 19:1, 3; 31:7). It is probably connected with the adjective *ʾĕlîl* “worthless, nothing” (Job 13:4; Zech 11:17) and sounds like *ʾēl* / *ʾĕlōhîm*, so the word itself mocks what it names (BDB; HALOT; Preuss, TDOT 1). The line keeps the standard “idols” (ASV, NRSV, NJPS) and leaves the wordplay to the apparatus (central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`, new). *yištaḥăwû* is “they bow down” (ASV “worship”), as in the central `hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship` entry at micah-woh 5:12, which shares the phrase “the work of your hands.” The plain verb leaves the reader to see from the context that the prostration is worship.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשַּׁ֥ח אָדָ֖ם וַיִּשְׁפַּל־אִ֑ישׁ וְאַל־תִּשָּׂ֖א לָהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: So humankind is bowed down, and man is brought low — and do not forgive them!
i18n.he: וַיִּשַּׁ֥ח אָדָ֖ם וַיִּשְׁפַּל־אִ֑ישׁ וְאַל־תִּשָּׂ֖א לָהֶֽם׃

notes.official:
*wayyiššaḥ ʾāḏām wayyišpal-ʾîš* “So humankind is bowed down, and man is brought low.” The pair returns as a refrain at 5:15. ASV reads it as a social contrast, “the mean man … the great man,” on the model of *bᵉnê ʾāḏām … bᵉnê ʾîš* in Ps 49:3. Without *bᵉnê* the two nouns are most naturally synonymous (NRSV “people … everyone”; NJPS “man … mortal”). The line renders them “humankind … man” (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`, new; the wave ruling on this pair awaits sign-off).

*wᵉʾal-tiśśāʾ lāhem* “and do not forgive them!”: *nśʾ* “lift, bear” with *lᵉ-* of the person is “forgive” (BDB; compare Gen 18:24, 26). Others read a statement, “and you cannot raise them up.” **Textual:** the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) lacks v. 9b and v. 10, and several commentators take the words as a later addition (Wildberger; Williamson). The line keeps MT (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: בּ֣וֹא בַצּ֔וּר וְהִטָּמֵ֖ן בֶּֽעָפָ֑ר מִפְּנֵי֙ פַּ֣חַד יְהוָ֔ה וּמֵהֲדַ֖ר גְּאֹנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Enter into the rock, and hide yourself in the dust, from before the terror of YHWH and from the splendor of his majesty.
i18n.he: בּ֣וֹא בַצּ֔וּר וְהִטָּמֵ֖ן בֶּֽעָפָ֑ר מִפְּנֵי֙ פַּ֣חַד יְהוָ֔ה וּמֵהֲדַ֖ר גְּאֹנֽוֹ׃

notes.official: *ûmēhăḏar gᵉʾōnô* “and from the splendor of his majesty” (also vv. 19, 21). ASV and NRSV have “the glory of his majesty.” In this project “glory” is the fixed English for *kāḇôḏ* (central `kavod-yhwh`), and Isaiah puts *kāḇôḏ* and *hāḏār* side by side in one verse (35:2). *hāḏār* therefore has its own word, “splendor,” as at 53:2 (“no splendor”), and *gāʾôn* is “majesty,” as at 24:14 (overlay `hadar-splendor-isaiah`, new). NJPS has “his dread majesty.” *paḥaḏ YHWH* is “the terror of YHWH.” *bôʾ baṣṣûr wᵉhiṭṭāmēn beʿāp̄ār* “Enter into the rock, and hide yourself in the dust”: the imperatives are singular and address each hearer. **Textual:** 1QIsaᵃ lacks this verse (see v. 9); the line keeps MT.

paragraphs.text: עֵינֵ֞י גַּבְה֤וּת אָדָם֙ שָׁפֵ֔ל וְשַׁ֖ח ר֣וּם אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְנִשְׂגַּ֧ב יְהוָ֛ה לְבַדּ֖וֹ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃ (ס)

i18n.en: The haughty eyes of humankind shall be brought low, and the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and YHWH alone shall be exalted in that day.
i18n.he: עֵינֵ֞י גַּבְה֤וּת אָדָם֙ שָׁפֵ֔ל וְשַׁ֖ח ר֣וּם אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְנִשְׂגַּ֧ב יְהוָ֛ה לְבַדּ֖וֹ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃ (ס)

notes.official: *ʿênê gaḇhûṯ ʾāḏām šāp̄ēl* “The haughty eyes of humankind shall be brought low,” literally “the eyes of the haughtiness of humankind.” The singular *šāp̄ēl* with a plural subject is a roughness of the Hebrew that the English does not reproduce. *gaḇhûṯ* and *rûm* are “haughty / haughtiness” and “loftiness” in both v. 11 and v. 17, where ASV varies its English, so the refrain repeats in English as it does in Hebrew. *ʾāḏām* is “humankind” and *ʾănāšîm* “men” (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`). *wᵉniśgaḇ YHWH lᵉḇaddô bayyôm hahûʾ* “and YHWH alone shall be exalted in that day” is the refrain of vv. 11 and 17.

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י י֞וֹם לַיהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת עַ֥ל כָּל־גֵּאֶ֖ה וָרָ֑ם וְעַ֖ל כָּל־נִשָּׂ֥א וְשָׁפֵֽל׃

i18n.en: For there is a day of YHWH of hosts upon all that is proud and lofty, and upon all that is lifted up — and it shall be brought low;
i18n.he: כִּ֣י י֞וֹם לַיהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת עַ֥ל כָּל־גֵּאֶ֖ה וָרָ֑ם וְעַ֖ל כָּל־נִשָּׂ֥א וְשָׁפֵֽל׃

notes.official:
*kî yôm laYHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* is literally “for YHWH of hosts has a day” (NRSV; NJPS “has ready a day”). The line keeps ASV’s structure, “For there is a day of YHWH of hosts,” which preserves the phrase “day of YHWH.” This is the book’s first use of the motif developed at 13:6, 9 (compare Amos 5:18–20). *YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* follows overlay `yhwh-tzevaot-hosts-isaiah`.

*wᵉšāp̄ēl* “and it shall be brought low” closes the verse. Many commentators emend to *wᵉḡāḇōah* “and high,” which gives three adjectives matching v. 13 (Wildberger; BHS apparatus). The LXX has a verb, “and they shall be humbled.” The line keeps MT (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

paragraphs.text: וְעַל֙ כָּל־אַרְזֵ֣י הַלְּבָנ֔וֹן הָרָמִ֖ים וְהַנִּשָּׂאִ֑ים וְעַ֖ל כָּל־אַלּוֹנֵ֥י הַבָּשָֽׁן׃

i18n.en: and upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan;
i18n.he: וְעַל֙ כָּל־אַרְזֵ֣י הַלְּבָנ֔וֹן הָרָמִ֖ים וְהַנִּשָּׂאִ֑ים וְעַ֖ל כָּל־אַלּוֹנֵ֥י הַבָּשָֽׁן׃

paragraphs.text: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־הֶהָרִ֣ים הָרָמִ֑ים וְעַ֖ל כָּל־הַגְּבָע֥וֹת הַנִּשָּׂאֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: and upon all the high mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up;
i18n.he: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־הֶהָרִ֣ים הָרָמִ֑ים וְעַ֖ל כָּל־הַגְּבָע֥וֹת הַנִּשָּׂאֽוֹת׃

paragraphs.text: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־מִגְדָּ֣ל גָּבֹ֑הַ וְעַ֖ל כָּל־חוֹמָ֥ה בְצוּרָֽה׃

i18n.en: and upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall;
i18n.he: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־מִגְדָּ֣ל גָּבֹ֑הַ וְעַ֖ל כָּל־חוֹמָ֥ה בְצוּרָֽה׃

paragraphs.text: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־אֳנִיּ֣וֹת תַּרְשִׁ֑ישׁ וְעַ֖ל כָּל־שְׂכִיּ֥וֹת הַחֶמְדָּֽה׃

i18n.en: and upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all the beautiful vessels.
i18n.he: וְעַ֖ל כָּל־אֳנִיּ֣וֹת תַּרְשִׁ֑ישׁ וְעַ֖ל כָּל־שְׂכִיּ֥וֹת הַחֶמְדָּֽה׃

notes.official:
*śᵉḵiyyôṯ haḥemdāh* is a crux, and the line departs from ASV here. ASV’s “pleasant imagery” derives the noun from *śkh* “look” (compare *maśkîṯ* “carved figure,” Lev 26:1). Modern lexica connect it with an Egyptian word for a ship, and the parallel “ships of Tarshish” in the first half of the verse supports that sense (HALOT; Wildberger; Blenkinsopp). NRSV has “the beautiful craft” and NJPS “the gallant barks”; the LXX already combines both ideas (“every sight of beautiful ships”). The line reads “all the beautiful vessels” (overlay `sekhiyyot-hachemdah-vessels-isaiah-2`, new; claim type inferred). “Vessels” keeps the word distinct from *ʾŏniyyôṯ* “ships” and stays in the language of seafaring. NRSV’s “craft” is avoided because present-day English also uses it of aircraft.

**Lens-salient site (apparatus note, not a translation claim).** A “craft” rendering of this verse can be read as describing flying vehicles. The Hebrew line is about ships: *ʾŏniyyôṯ taršîš* are the large merchant ships of the Mediterranean trade (1 Kgs 10:22), and the parallel noun is read in the same sea-going sense. The canon does not cite this verse.

paragraphs.text: וְשַׁח֙ גַּבְה֣וּת הָאָדָ֔ם וְשָׁפֵ֖ל ר֣וּם אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְנִשְׂגַּ֧ב יְהוָ֛ה לְבַדּ֖וֹ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃

i18n.en: And the haughtiness of humankind shall be bowed down, and the loftiness of men shall be brought low; and YHWH alone shall be exalted in that day.
i18n.he: וְשַׁח֙ גַּבְה֣וּת הָאָדָ֔ם וְשָׁפֵ֖ל ר֣וּם אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וְנִשְׂגַּ֧ב יְהוָ֛ה לְבַדּ֖וֹ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃

notes.official: The refrain of v. 11 returns with its verbs exchanged: *šaḥ* “bowed down” now goes with *gaḇhûṯ* and *šāp̄ēl* “brought low” with *rûm*. The English keeps the same nouns and verbs, so the chiasm is visible (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: וְהָאֱלִילִ֖ים כָּלִ֥יל יַחֲלֹֽף׃

i18n.en: And the idols shall utterly pass away.
i18n.he: וְהָאֱלִילִ֖ים כָּלִ֥יל יַחֲלֹֽף׃

notes.official: *wᵉhāʾĕlîlîm kālîl yaḥălōp̄* “And the idols shall utterly pass away.” *kālîl* “wholly” echoes the sound of *ʾĕlîlîm*, a pun English cannot keep (central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`). The verb is singular with the plural subject; the line renders the sense.

paragraphs.text: וּבָ֙אוּ֙ בִּמְעָר֣וֹת צֻרִ֔ים וּבִמְחִלּ֖וֹת עָפָ֑ר מִפְּנֵ֞י פַּ֤חַד יְהוָה֙ וּמֵהֲדַ֣ר גְּאוֹנ֔וֹ בְּקוּמ֖וֹ לַעֲרֹ֥ץ הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And they shall go into the caves of the rocks and into the holes of the dust, from before the terror of YHWH and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
i18n.he: וּבָ֙אוּ֙ בִּמְעָר֣וֹת צֻרִ֔ים וּבִמְחִלּ֖וֹת עָפָ֑ר מִפְּנֵ֞י פַּ֤חַד יְהוָה֙ וּמֵהֲדַ֣ר גְּאוֹנ֔וֹ בְּקוּמ֖וֹ לַעֲרֹ֥ץ הָאָֽרֶץ׃

notes.official:
*laʿărōṣ hāʾāreṣ* “to terrify the earth” (also v. 21) is a sound-play on *ʿrṣ* and *ʾereṣ* that English cannot keep. ASV has “to shake mightily the earth.” *ʿāraṣ* means “to terrify, inspire awe” (BDB; HALOT), the sense it has elsewhere in Isaiah (8:12–13; 29:23; 47:12). NRSV has “to terrify the earth” and NJPS “to overawe the earth”; the line follows NRSV (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

*mᵉḥillôṯ ʿāp̄ār* is “holes of the dust,” keeping *ʿāp̄ār* “dust” as in v. 10 (ASV “holes of the earth”). The subject of *ûḇāʾû* is “they,” as in MT; ASV supplies “men.” “The earth” is the universal scope of the day of YHWH (overlay `eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24`, extended to vv. 19 and 21). On “the splendor of his majesty” see v. 10.

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֤וֹם הַהוּא֙ יַשְׁלִ֣יךְ הָאָדָ֔ם אֵ֚ת אֱלִילֵ֣י כַסְפּ֔וֹ וְאֵ֖ת אֱלִילֵ֣י זְהָב֑וֹ אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָֽשׂוּ־לוֹ֙ לְהִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֔ת לַחְפֹּ֥ר פֵּר֖וֹת וְלָעֲטַלֵּפִֽים׃

i18n.en: In that day humankind shall cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to bow down to, to the moles and to the bats,
i18n.he: בַּיּ֤וֹם הַהוּא֙ יַשְׁלִ֣יךְ הָאָדָ֔ם אֵ֚ת אֱלִילֵ֣י כַסְפּ֔וֹ וְאֵ֖ת אֱלִילֵ֣י זְהָב֑וֹ אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָֽשׂוּ־לוֹ֙ לְהִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֔ת לַחְפֹּ֥ר פֵּר֖וֹת וְלָעֲטַלֵּפִֽים׃

notes.official:
*laḥpōr pērôṯ* is printed as two words in the Leningrad Codex, “to dig holes.” The WLC text carries no ketiv/qere note at this word. Many Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient versions read one word, *laḥăp̄arpērôṯ*, the name of a burrowing animal paired with “the bats” (BDB; BHS apparatus). ASV and NRSV (“moles”) and NJPS (“flying foxes”) translate it so. The consonants are the same and only the word division differs. The line follows the one-word reading, “to the moles.” Because this departs from the Leningrad word division, it is reported under overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah` and listed for sign-off (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2`).

*ʾăšer ʿāśû-lô* “which they made for themselves”: the plural verb has an indefinite subject, and *lô* refers to the collective *hāʾāḏām* (NRSV; ASV “which have been made for them”). *ʾĕlîlîm* “idols” and *lᵉhištaḥăwōṯ* “to bow down to” are rendered as in v. 8 (central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`, `hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship`); *hāʾāḏām* is “humankind” (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: לָבוֹא֙ בְּנִקְר֣וֹת הַצֻּרִ֔ים וּבִסְעִפֵ֖י הַסְּלָעִ֑ים מִפְּנֵ֞י פַּ֤חַד יְהוָה֙ וּמֵהֲדַ֣ר גְּאוֹנ֔וֹ בְּקוּמ֖וֹ לַעֲרֹ֥ץ הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: to go into the clefts of the rocks and into the crevices of the crags, from before the terror of YHWH and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
i18n.he: לָבוֹא֙ בְּנִקְר֣וֹת הַצֻּרִ֔ים וּבִסְעִפֵ֖י הַסְּלָעִ֑ים מִפְּנֵ֞י פַּ֤חַד יְהוָה֙ וּמֵהֲדַ֣ר גְּאוֹנ֔וֹ בְּקוּמ֖וֹ לַעֲרֹ֥ץ הָאָֽרֶץ׃

notes.official: *bᵉniqrôṯ haṣṣurîm ûḇisʿip̄ê hassᵉlāʿîm* “into the clefts of the rocks and into the crevices of the crags” varies the “caves of the rocks … holes of the dust” of v. 19. The refrain then closes as in v. 19 (“the splendor of his majesty,” “to terrify the earth”), under the same entries.

paragraphs.text: חִדְל֤וּ לָכֶם֙ מִן־הָ֣אָדָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר נְשָׁמָ֖ה בְּאַפּ֑וֹ כִּֽי־בַמֶּ֥ה נֶחְשָׁ֖ב הֽוּא׃ (פ)

i18n.en: Cease from humankind, who has breath in his nostrils; for of what account is he?
i18n.he: חִדְל֤וּ לָכֶם֙ מִן־הָ֣אָדָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר נְשָׁמָ֖ה בְּאַפּ֑וֹ כִּֽי־בַמֶּ֥ה נֶחְשָׁ֖ב הֽוּא׃ (פ)

notes.official:
**Textual:** the verse is absent from the Old Greek (LXX), and several commentators take it as a later comment on vv. 6–21 (Wildberger). The line keeps MT (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*ḥiḏlû lāḵem min-hāʾāḏām* is literally “cease for yourselves from humankind.” The line keeps the bare “Cease from” and supplies no object such as trust or praise (NRSV “Turn away from mortals”; NJPS “Oh, cease to glorify man”). *ʾăšer nᵉšāmāh bᵉʾappô* “who has breath in his nostrils” recalls Gen 2:7 in wording. The central `neshamah-chayim` entry is scoped to that verse and is not applied. The singular pronouns follow the Hebrew, where *hāʾāḏām* is collective (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`). *kî-ḇammeh neḥšāḇ hûʾ* is “for of what account is he?”
